content: The provided text is a detailed compilation of studies examining the relationship between household crowding and various health outcomes. 1. Doshi et al. (2015, Bangladesh): This study focused on children aged 12–59 months. It investigated the association between influenza and household crowding, defined as four or more individuals (including the child) sleeping in the same room. The study employed a case-control design with 145 influenza cases and 341 controls. 2. Gares et al.: This study examined the relationship between Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection and household crowding, defined as five rooms per person. It utilized a cohort design with a sample size of 12,457 participants. 3. Hegab et al.: This cross-sectional study explored the prevalence of scabies in households with five persons per room. The study included 92 cases of scabies. 4. Howie et al. (2016, Gambia): This case-control study investigated the impact of household crowding, measured as persons per room, on pneumonia in children aged 2–59 months. The study included 458 cases of severe pneumonia, 322 cases of non-severe pneumonia, and 801 neighborhood controls. 5. Hughes et al. (2017, USA): This secondary analysis of the 2011 American Housing Survey examined asthma prevalence in households with children aged 6–17 years. Crowding was defined as more than two persons per bedroom. The study analyzed data from 33,201 households. 6. Kumar et al. (2015, India): This cross-sectional study assessed the relationship between household crowding (defined as more than one person per room) and Helicobacter pylori infection. The study included 7,398 participants. 7. Mirabel et al. (2015, New Caledonia): This case-control study investigated the association between rheumatic heart disease and household crowding, defined as three or more persons per room. The study included 114 cases and 227 controls. 8. Olea et al. (2017, Chile): This case-control study examined meningococcal disease in households with five persons per bedroom. Cases were identified through the Ministry of Health monitoring system, and controls were selected from the same municipalities. The study included 135 cases and 618 controls. 9. Romani et al. (2017, Fiji): This cross-sectional study, conducted as a baseline for a trial, investigated scabies and impetigo in six island communities. Crowding was defined as four or more persons per room compared to one person per room. The study included 2,051 participants. 10. Sinha et al. (2015, India): This cross-sectional study explored allergic rhinitis in adults aged 30 years or older. Crowding was defined as more than two persons per room or less than 110 square feet for two persons. The study included 1,203 participants. 11. Tin et al. (2016, New Zealand): This cohort study examined acute respiratory infections in children under one year, aged 1–2 years, and those with two or more persons per bedroom. The study included 6,112 participants. 12. Tse et al. (2016, Canada): This cross-sectional study investigated severe respiratory infections in Inuit children aged 3–5 years. Crowding was measured as persons per room on a continuous scale. The study included 388 participants. 13. Verani et al. (2016, South Africa): This case-control study examined presumed bacterial pneumonia in HIV-negative children. Crowding was defined as more than two persons sleeping in the same room as the child. The study included 889 cases and 2,628 controls. 14. Vieira et al. (2016, Brazil): This case-control study investigated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in HIV-infected youth under 25 years. Crowding was defined as five or more persons per household. The study included 117 participants. 15. Vincenti-Gonzalez et al.: This cross-sectional study examined dengue virus in households with five persons per room. The study included 1,985 participants. 16. Weber et al. (2017, Germany): This cross-sectional study investigated respiratory problems in children living in households with more than one person per room (including the kitchen but excluding the bathroom) or less than 20 square meters of living space per person. The study included 4,732 participants. 17. Monasta et al. (2008, Italy): This cross-sectional study examined diarrheal diseases in children aged 0–4 years living in informal settlements with five persons per room. The study included 165 participants. 18. Abu Mourad et al. (2004, West Bank and Gaza Strip): This cross-sectional study investigated diarrheal diseases and intestinal parasites in households with four or more persons per room. The study included 1,655 participants. 19. Etiler et al. (2004, Turkey): This prospective cohort study examined overall and persistent diarrhea in children under 12 months. Crowding was defined as three persons per room compared to one person per room. The study included 204 participants. 20. Okour et al. (2012, Jordan): This cross-sectional study investigated diarrhea in children aged 0–13 years living in residential housing with two persons per room. The study included 197 participants. 21. El-Gilany et al. (2005, Egypt): This cross-sectional study examined diarrhea prevalence in children aged 0–5 years. Crowding was defined as more than three persons per room compared to less than three persons per room. The study included 4,458 participants. 22. Pezzani et al. (2012, Argentina): This cross-sectional study investigated parasitic infections in children aged 3–17 years living in residential housing with more than three persons per room. The study included 716 participants. 23. Ferrer et al. (2008, Brazil): This case-control study examined diarrhea in children aged 0–10 years. Crowding was defined as more than three persons per room compared to less than three persons per room. The study included 1,688 cases and 1,676 controls. 24. Kyle et al. (2011, United Kingdom): This retrospective cohort study investigated emergency admissions due to diarrhea in children aged 0–14 years. Crowding was defined using the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) definition. The study included 24,481 participants. 25. Perry et al. (2005, USA): This prospective cohort study examined secondary transmission of gastroenteritis in households where individuals shared a bed with a primary gastroenteritis patient. The study included 5,015 participants. 26. Quigley et al. (2006, United Kingdom): This case-control study investigated diarrhea in children under 12 months. Crowding was defined as more than one person per room compared to less than one person per room. The study included 167 cases and 137 controls. 27. Harper et al. (2015, Canada): This cross-sectional study examined acute gastrointestinal illness in Inuit households experiencing overcrowding. The study included 1,517 participants. 28. Mohan et al. (2017, multiple countries): This cohort study investigated rotavirus infection and diarrhea in children under two years. Crowding was defined as more than two persons per room. The study included 1,737 children contributing 22,646 surveillance records and 7,440 diarrheal specimens. 29. Ramani et al. (2017, India): This cross-sectional study examined diarrhea in adolescents in a school environment. Crowding was defined as less than two, two to less than four, and four or more persons per room. The study included 114 participants. 30. Faisal-Cury et al. (2009, Brazil): This cross-sectional study investigated common mental disorders in women living in residential housing with seven or more persons per room. The study included 831 participants. 31. Riva et al.: This cross-sectional study examined feelings of anxiety and depression in individuals living in residential housing with more than one person per room. The study included 3,066 participants. 32. Kimhy et al. (2006, Israel): This retrospective cohort study investigated schizophrenia in individuals living in residential housing with more than three persons per room compared to less than one person per room. The study included 11,015 participants. 33. Cabieses et al. (2012, Chile): This cross-sectional study examined psychiatric disability in individuals living in residential housing with more than one person per room. The study included 2,688 participants. 34. Regoeczi et al. (2008, Canada): This prospective cohort study investigated depression, aggression, and withdrawal in individuals living in residential housing. The study included 1,018 participants in the final analysis. 35. Barnes et al. (2011, United Kingdom): This retrospective cohort study examined feelings of unhappiness about health in children aged 5–18 years living in overcrowded housing for varying durations. The study included 6,341 participants. 36. Al-Hemiary et al. (2015, Iraq): This cross-sectional study investigated alcohol and drug abuse in individuals living in households with two or more persons per room. The study included 2,678 participants. 37. Firdous et al. (2017, India): This cross-sectional study examined psychological distress in adults aged 18 years or older living in overcrowded households. The study included 4,326 households. 38. Gray et al. (2016, Canada): This cross-sectional study investigated mental health in Inuit youth aged 15–30 years. Crowding was measured as the number of people divided by the number of bedrooms plus two. The study included 452 participants. 39. Pierse et al. (2016, New Zealand): This cross-sectional study examined psychological distress in adults aged 18–80 years. Crowding was defined based on the number of bedrooms available versus required. The study included over 13,800 responses in a longitudinal study. 40. Waters et al.: This cohort study investigated autonomic nervous system reactivity and externalizing behavior problems in families with five persons per room. The study included 99 families. 41. Chambers et al.: This cross-sectional study examined sleep disorders, including difficulty falling asleep and self-reported sleep quality, in individuals living in overcrowded households. The study included 371 participants. 42. Johnson et al. (2015, USA): This ecological study investigated sleep disorders in adults with sleep-disordered breathing. Crowding was measured as the percentage of households in a census tract with more than one person per room. The study included 1,789 participants. 43. Van der Spuy et al. (2017, Canada): This cross-sectional study examined excessive daytime sleepiness in two First Nation communities. Crowding was defined as more than one person per room. The study included 874 participants.
